newsitem.title: USA: Government, defense rest in NYC mob case.
newsitem.headline: Government, defense rest in NYC mob case.

text.p: Attorneys for accused mob boss Vincent "The Chin" Gigante rested their defence of the reputed head of the Genovese crime family on Monday without calling a single witness in his murder and racketeering trial.
But they did present statements made at a 1986 trial in which a federal prosecutor referred to Anthony "Fat Tony" Salerno, and not Gigante, as the head of the New York-based organised crime family.

Gigante, facing a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment, is accused of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of Mafia protocol such as unauthorised slayings.
Gigante's attorneys have claimed he is incapacitated by mental illness. He is known for wandering the neighbourhood around his Greenwich Village apartment in a tattered bathrobe.
On Monday his attorneys read a list of dates to the jury of the times Gigante was hospitalized prior to the filing of the 1993 indictment.
Authorities say he has feigned mental illness to avoid prosecution.
The prosecution rested its case earlier Monday after calling a string of government informants to testify.

The defence called for a mistrial, saying the government had not proved its case beyond hearsay testimony from the former mobsters-turned-informants. But U.S. District Court Judge Jack Weinstein denied the defence motion.

Among the informants to testify against Gigante was Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano, a mob turncoat whose testimony was key in the 1992 murder and racketeering conviction of Gambino godfather John Gotti. Gotti is serving a life prison term without possibility of parole.
Closing arguments in the Gigante case were expected to begin on Tuesday and jury deliberations could begin on Wednesday.

The statements pointing to Salerno, and not Gigante, as head of the Genovese crime family came from the 1986 commission trial, when the then reputed heads of New York's five crime families were indicted on an array of federal charges.
Eight defendants were convicted in that case, and each sentenced to 100 years in prison.
If convicted, Gigante faces a possible life term.
